title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: New federal bills on water and energy reporting land amid 55% statewide opposition to local projects.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy. Today we're digging into a fresh push from Washington that could reshape how these projects get built right here at home.

That's right, Emmy. Yesterday U.S. Representative Hillary Scholten introduced federal legislation requiring annual reporting on data centers' water and energy use, plus updates to Defense Department cooling standards to safeguard water supplies.
This comes just a day after a poll showed 55 percent of Michigan primary voters oppose data centers near their homes, with even higher numbers among Democrats. Why is she stepping in now, Graham?

Scholten represents Grand Rapids and has watched the local fights play out in Kent County and beyond. Her bills aim to create transparency that local officials say they've been missing when companies pitch these campuses.
So what exactly would the reporting cover? Is this just paperwork or does it change how projects get approved?

It mandates yearly surveys of resource consumption and ties into broader efficiency rules. The idea is to give communities real numbers on power draw and water use before they commit tax breaks or grid upgrades.
That sounds like it could help places like Lowell, where the council just killed talks with Microsoft over secrecy on those exact issues. How does this federal step connect to those local decisions?

It doesn't override local zoning, but it could arm residents and officials with data they can use in their own reviews. We've seen similar pushes in other states where towns felt blindsided by the scale of demand.
And the poll from Sunday really drives home the stakes. Fifty-five percent opposition statewide, jumping to 63 percent among likely Democratic primary voters. What are people most worried about?

Electric bills, water availability, and whether the tax revenue actually offsets the strain on local infrastructure. Candidates are already clashing over who ends up paying if these big loads come online.
DTE Energy said yesterday that landing these data centers is key to holding rates steady. If projects stall, does that mean higher bills for everyone else?

That's the utility's argument in their latest filing. They see the big loads as a way to spread costs, but residents in places like Washtenaw County are already filing recalls over exactly those concerns.
Seven officials facing recall bids there after yesterday's signature turn-in. How far back does this tension go in Michigan?
It's been building for months across multiple counties. Townships have paused projects, voters are organizing, and now we're seeing federal attention because the local fights are getting intense.
What happens next with Scholten's bills? Do they have a real shot or is this more messaging?

They're newly introduced, so the immediate impact is spotlighting the issue. Any movement would likely take months, but it signals to Michigan communities that Washington is watching the resource demands.

Meanwhile on the ground, Wayne County just got a six-billion-dollar proposal today that could bring thousands of construction jobs but also heavy electricity needs. Local officials haven't scheduled a review yet.
That's a massive scale. Tax revenue gains are possible, but so is grid strain that could affect rates for nearby homes.
And in Genesee County they delayed an environmental vote on Saturday, giving residents more time to review traffic, power, and noise impacts.
Extra weeks for public input there, which matches what we've seen in other spots where communities want breathing room.
Otsego went further on Saturday and banned new data centers for a full year. That pause lets them shape rules around noise and infrastructure before anything moves forward.
Dowagiac is shifting an existing site from Bitcoin mining to a twenty-megawatt AI contract under a ten-year deal that could top a billion dollars, though noise litigation from residents continues.

And U.S. Senate candidate John James said Saturday he'd leave siting and tax decisions to local officials rather than add state rules. How does that land with voters in counties already fighting these projects?
It puts the focus back on townships like Saline and Coldwater where power, water, and tax break debates are already active. Primary voters decide today whether that resonates.
With the poll showing broad opposition, local control might be exactly what many want right now.
Exactly. The federal reporting could complement that by giving everyone better facts to work with.
So pulling it together, Scholten's move and the Sunday poll both point to a moment where transparency and local say are front and center.
And with projects still landing like the Wayne County proposal, those conversations aren't slowing down.
No major meetings on the calendar for tonight or tomorrow that we've confirmed, but we'll keep watching the tracker for any updates.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Scholten Pushes Federal Data Center Oversight as Michigan Voters Push Back
